title: The Joyful Nerdiness of a 66-Hour, Nonstop Reading of ‘The Power Broker’
summary: New Yorkers read the 1,162-page book around the clock for four days, reflecting on the legacy of Robert Moses and celebrating its author, Robert Caro, who read the final pages.

There was a union organizer who had spent the day meeting with biology researchers in Manhattan. There was a biographer of Albert Einstein who had just returned from a reporting trip to New Mexico. There was a “street librarian” from the Bronx who arrived in Brooklyn by subway and Uber after 1 a.m.


There was a descendant of a Depression-era mayor, several current government officials, a few college professors and the voice of the subway announcements.


Each climbed to the third floor of a cavernous space in an old brick building that was once a paint factory to read about 1,300 words of what has been celebrated as one of the best American nonfiction books: Robert Caro’s “The Power Broker.”


Over 66 hours, hundreds of people took turns onstage reading aloud from the monumental 1974 book chronicling the life and projects of Robert Moses, the polarizing great builder who is responsible for much of modern New York City.


At 9 p.m. on Thursday, there was wine and a picked-over charcuterie board as readers recited passages about Mr. Moses’s childhood. At midnight the next night, there were scenes about his penchant for retribution and the 255 playgrounds he built in the 1930s.


And all throughout, there was Mr. Caro’s rhythmic and mesmerizing prose and the torrent of vivid details uncovered by his obsessive reporting.
